highlights: Oral peptide enhancers act in a micro-niche; a mechanistic model quantifies it
Paired Monte Carlo arms isolate what co-localization adds to bioavailability
Variance-based sensitivity ranks niche thickness and enhancer potency first
Spatial and stagnant-layer models test whether the predicted advantage survives
Failure boundaries give measurable pass-fail criteria for the first experiments
abstract: Oral absolute bioavailability of 2 to 4 kDa peptides stays near 1%. The best-characterized enhancer tablet acts only where and when enhancer, peptide and protection coincide, which suggests that the architecture of the dosage form is a design variable. We built a mechanistic Monte Carlo model of a co-localized, reversible permeation-enhancer and efflux-modulator architecture (Dual-Lock) with explicit mass balances, evidence-graded and correlated priors, and asked when it would raise bioavailability to at least 4% with reversible epithelial exposure. All arms shared the same random draws, so that ablations and negative controls isolate each component. Global sensitivity analysis, benefit-risk analysis, falsification maps, alternative transport models, observation-conditioned analysis and comparison with published human data tested robustness.

With the reference calibrated to 1.2%, Dual-Lock reached a median of 5.0% at half the enhancer dose and met the target with reversible exposure in 45% of draws against 15% for the reference. Confinement accounted for most of the benefit (removing it cost 41 points of success) but required a self-limiting enhancer to remain reversible. Output uncertainty was shared among peptide biology, enhancer pharmacology and architecture. The advantage persisted in every transport structure that reproduced the baseline, but fell to 22% if the reference performs like oral semaglutide, and the upper tail and the enhancer-dose response disagreed with published data. Failure boundaries (niche thickness above 0.6 cm, an unmixed niche, a matrix-only gain above 3-fold) define the first experiments. The results are conditional on author-assigned priors and are not evidence that any formulation works.
keywords: Oral peptide delivery; Permeation enhancer; Efflux modulation; Monte Carlo simulation; Global sensitivity analysis; Falsifiability
